newsitem.title: UK: Muted dlr gives up early gains at Euro midsession.
newsitem.headline: Muted dlr gives up early gains at Euro midsession.

text.p: The dollar failed to hold on to early gains notched up after news of U.S. military intervention in Iraq as dealers eyed further developments in the Gulf and awaited fresh economic data.
After a predictable spike up in oil prices and the dollar dealers took profits from the dollar's early bout of strength.

"The markets seem to feel that this situation is not going to escalate much more," said David Bloom, currency economist at HSBC James Capel. "It has helped boost the dollar initially but the focus is now back on economic data."

The dollar reached a high of 1.4912 marks in a wave of early safe-haven buying and rose to 109.45 yen. At 1032 GMT it was back down at 1.4863/68 marks and 109.18/28 yen, little changed from 1.4863/70 and 109.10/18 at Monday's European close.
The dollar's initially firmer tone was also helped by an article in the Wall Street Journal predicting a near-term U.S. interest rate rise, analysts said.

The newspaper said the Federal Reserve were moving toward a sharper-than-expected rate increase unless clear signs of slower growth appear in the next three weeks. The next meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee is on September 24.

Analysts attributed the lack of follow-through buying on the Iraq news to concerns that higher oil prices might spook the bond markets. Brent crude oil shot up to post-Gulf war highs of $23.50 per barrel before settling at $22.67 at 1035 GMT. to news like that, but the positive effects for the dollar are being diluted by the potentially negative response of the bond market," said Paul Meggyesi, senior currency economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Equally, the bond market's dislike of rising interest rates, has also tended to hurt the dollar, said Meggyesi.
Analysts also noted that apart from short-lived spikes higher, the dollar has not managed to sustain its gains from similar situations in the past.
After the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait in August 1990, oil prices jumped to a high of over $40, and the dollar gained almost two pfennigs in the two days after the annexation.
In the following two weeks, it lost five pfennigs and as oil prices subsided from their peak, the dollar resumed its slide to below 1.50 marks by early 1991.
An address to the nation by U.S. President Bill Clinton at 1200 GMT will be eyed for further developments, traders said.
At 1400 GMT, the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) releases its August survey.

Traders are bracing themselves for another strong figure after a robust Chicago purchasing managers' survey last week, which came on the heels of an upward revision in U.S. second-quarter GDP growth and strong home sales data.
Analysts polled by Reuters expected, on average, a NAPM rise to 52.9 after slipping to 50.2 in July.
But after the Chicago data, Bloom now expected the NAPM could reach as high as 54.
With U.S. July leading indicators also released at 1230 GMT, and August auto sales data due later in the day, U.S. bonds could face another difficult day, dealers said.
Peripheral European currencies and the French franc gained some relief from the Iraqi news. Currencies associated with oil price swings, such as sterling, notched initial gains.
The pound dropped back from a high of 2.3264 marks to trade at 2.3208/18, up from 2.3186/97 late here on Monday. Against the dollar, it was at $1.5608/16 versus $1.5595/5600 yesterday.
But the yen remained fairly stable despite Japan's dependency on oil imports. -London newsroom +44 171 542 7792
